newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine debt restructuring claimed a success.
newsitem.headline: Philippine debt restructuring claimed a success.

text.p: The Philippines' recent successful debt restructuring schemes have validated international confidence in the country, officials and analysts said after the issue of its maiden 10-year bond on Tuesday.

The 10-year fixed-rate Treasury bond, which fetched a coupon rate of 16 percent, was oversubscribed. The government received bids worth 9.915 billion pesos ($377 million), while the offer was worth just two-billion pesos ($76 million).
"It's a success," Treasurer Caridad Valdehuesa said.

Deputy treasurer Eduardo Mendiola said major financial players swamped the auction, pushing the coupon to 16.0 percent, just 25 basis points higher than the seven-year fixed rate bonds which were auctioned in July.
"We are getting better entrenched in the international capital market," said Johnny Noe Ravalo, chief economist of the Bankers Association of the Philippines.

He said the 10-year peso bonds as well as the recent issue of 20-year uncollateralised Brady bonds had shown that the present economic liberalisation programmes being undertaken by the government are fully supported by foreign investors.
The new uncollateralised bonds were issued on Monday as part of the government's Brady exchange programme.
The Philippines issued $690 million worth of Brady bonds in exchange for $635 million worth of collateralised bonds and another $137 million outright sale of the bonds.
The bonds are priced 2.25 percentage points over the benchmark U.S. Treasuries, significantly lower than Mexico's 20-year bonds which were priced 4.45 percentage points over U.S. Treasuries.

"It is fascinating how quickly the Philippines has improved its credit story," Peter Woicke, regional executive of J.P. Morgan for Asia, said in a statement. J.P. Morgan is the lead arranger of the Brady exchange programme.

"When we lead-managed the country's debut three-year Eurobond in 1993, we could not have expected that by the time that bond matured in 1996, the country would be raising 20-year money from institutional investors," Woicke added.
The Philippines was shunned by the private capital market in the 1980s after it declared a debt payment moratorium in 1983.
Project financing was limited to multilateral financing which started to dwindle when eastern European countries begun to restructure their economies after the fall of Communism in the late 1980s.
The government used to issue Treasury bills of up to one year as investors were wary to invest beyond that due to the volatile political and economic situation.
In 1992, President Fidel Ramos started a wide-ranging liberalisation programme which opened up services and manufacturing industries to foreign investors.
The Bureau of Treasury started offering two-year fixed rate bonds in 1994, five-year bonds in 1995, and seven-year bonds in 1996. It has offered more than 110 billion pesos worth of bonds so far.
"The financial market is looking at our economic and financial system on a longer term basis ... And they see the rates going down in the long run," Treasurer Valdehuesa said.

"It will take years to reap the dividends (of these projects). But we believe there is ample dividend enough in the impact of modern infrastructure on the economy as a whole -- for this will not fail to yield returns for our core businesses in the group," he said.
The conglomerate's flagship Ayala Land Inc is the leader in the real estate sector.
It also has stakes in the telecommunications, food manufacturing, insurance and information technology sectors.
"The Ayala Group is harnessing its capabilities as a group of companies to bring to bear a synergistic approach to private sector involvement in economic development," he said.
Ayala said the country's current economic boom can be sustained if the policies of deregulation and liberalisation were continued.
"Philippine development can be sustained if we can maintain these policies of reform and institutionalise rigour in their implementation," said Ayala, a doyen of Filipino industrialists.
